title: Russian jets killed civilians fleeing across the Euphrates, Syrian opposition says
text: Military jets thought to be Russian killed at least 60 civilians who were trying to escape heavy fighting in Syria's oil-rich Deir al Zor province when their small boats were hit as they tried to cross the Euphrates River, opposition activists, former residents and a war monitor said late on Wednesday. According to them, the jets struck makeshift rubber dinghies and boats carrying dozens of families fleeing the town of al Ashara, which lies on the western banks of the Euphrates south of Deir al Zor city, the provincial capital. The cities, towns and farms in the fertile strip along the Euphrates bordering Iraq, Islamic State's last major stronghold, are rapidly becoming the focus of Syria's six-year-long civil war. Russian jets carried out a second wave of strikes on the boats crossing the river, causing more casualties among people who rushed to rescue earlier survivors, said Abdullah al Akaidat, a tribal figure in northern Syria from Al Ashara who is in touch with relatives in the area. Russia is putting its military weight behind the Syrian army's campaign to retake the province bordering Iraq, racing U.S.-backed forces to seize territory from Islamic State. Last year U.S. coalition jets destroyed bridges linking villages on the northeast of the Euphrates river with towns on the opposite bank. Although the aim was to cut militant supply lines, this forced people to use ferries to cross the river and its tributaries and severed a major lifeline for civilians, pushing up the prices of goods and food. Fifteen civilians were killed in air strikes over the last 24 hours on the town of al Quriya, just further north of Ashara along the river, former residents in contact with relatives said.

title: C.E.O.s Running Prisons? Trump-Era Privatization Could Come at a Steep Cost
text: Last summer, the Justice Department chose to begin phasing out its use of private prisons. In a memo, Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Nor did they offer the kind of rehabilitation programs shown to cut recidivism. And they are especially dangerous. A recent report from the department’s inspector general found that inmates in private facilities, which hold some 12 percent of federal prisoners, were far more likely to have weapons. But privatization is likely to sweep through far more than prisons.

title: Hillary Clinton and Tim Kaine Release New Tax Returns, Pressing Donald Trump
text: Hillary Clinton and her running mate, Tim Kaine, made public another batch of their own income tax returns on Friday, increasing the pressure on her opponent, Donald J. Trump, to start releasing his own. The latest tax return of Mrs. Clinton and her husband, former President Bill Clinton, showed adjusted gross income of $10.6 million for 2015, a steep fall from earlier years but still enough to put them in the top 0.1 percent of American households. They paid around $3.6 million in federal taxes, an effective tax rate of about 35 percent. More than half of their income came from speeches; Mrs. Clinton also earned $3 million from “Hard Choices,” her memoir about her time as secretary of state. Mr. Kaine, the Virginia senator, and his wife, Anne Holton, who served as Virginia’s secretary of education until she stepped down last month, reported income of $313,441 for 2015. But beyond their earnings, the release was meant to highlight Mr. Trump’s refusal to release his own returns. Mike Pence, the Indiana governor and Mr. Trump’s running mate, has not released his tax data during the campaign either. Mrs. Clinton’s spokeswoman, Jennifer Palmieri, said in a statement that the release sets a “stark contrast” with Mr. Trump, whom she accused of “hiding behind fake excuses.” “He has failed to provide the public with the most basic financial information disclosed by every major candidate in the last 40 years,” she said. “What is he trying to hide?” The Trump campaign would not discuss his tax returns, but on Friday a spokesman, Jason Miller, issued a statement about Mrs. Clinton.

title: Saudi-led coalition to keep Yemen port open; air strikes kill at least nine
text: The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday that it would keep the Houthi-held port of Hodeidah, a vital route for aid, open for a month in spite of a new missile attack on Riyadh, but it continued air strikes that killed at least nine people. The Western-backed coalition, which controls access to Yemen's airspace and ports, said last month that it would let humanitarian relief through Hodeidah after a blockade of nearly three weeks that it imposed following a missile attack aimed at the Saudi capital's international airport. The Saudis say the Red Sea port, Yemen's main entry point for food and humanitarian supplies, is also used by the Houthis as a hub for bringing in weapons, which they accuse Iran of supplying. Tehran rejects the charges. On Wednesday, the coalition confirmed that it would keep the port accessible despite another Houthi missile attack on Riyadh on Tuesday, which Saudi forces also intercepted. “Keen to maintain humanitarian aid to the brotherly Yemeni people and as a result of intensified inspection measures, the coalition command announces that Hodeidah port will remain open for humanitarian and relief supplies,” the coalition said in a statement carried by the Saudi state news agency on Wednesday. title: U.S. to widen refugee program for Central Americans escaping violence
text: The United States will broaden its program assisting the thousands of people fleeing violence in El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry said on Wednesday. The announcement comes after a backlash from Democrats in the U.S. Congress, who urged the Obama administration to stop deporting families who fled the three crime-ridden Central American countries and entered the United States without documents. The expanded Refugee Admissions Program would provide “a safe and legal alternative to the dangerous journey many are currently tempted to begin, making them easy prey for human smugglers who have no interest but their own profits,” Kerry said in a speech at the National Defense University. President Barack Obama had previously said the United States would accept 3,000 refugees from Latin America by October this year. A State Department spokesperson said the administration has no plans to take in more than 3,000 refugees from the region, but that it may change the figure “should conditions require.” He said the U.S. government would work with the United Nations and non-governmental organizations to identify people needing refugee protection, singling out those targeted by criminal gangs, including human rights activists. “We also continue to explore additional options, including for those who may be at imminent risk of harm,” Kerry said. According to the State Department, once the United Nations High Commissioner on Human Rights refers a potential refugee to the United States for resettlement, the case is reviewed at a Resettlement Support Center. The United States runs nine such centers worldwide, but only one is in the Western hemisphere - in Quito, Ecuador. The State Department spokesperson said the Quito center has a branch office in San Salvador, El Salvador.

text: U.S. immigration authorities arrested hundreds of undocumented immigrants in at least a half-dozen states this week in a wave of raids marking the first large-scale enforcement of President Trump's Jan. 26 order to crack down on the estimated 11 million immigrants living here illegally. ICE dislikes the word raids and prefers to say authorities are carrying out targeted enforcement actions. Christensen said the raids, which started Monday and ended Friday at noon, found undocumented immigrants from a dozen Latin American countries. “We're talking about people who are threats to public safety or a threat to the integrity of the immigration system,” she said, noting that most of those detained were serious criminals, including some convicted of murder and domestic violence.

title: New York lawmakers set to open the door to mixed martial arts bouts
text: New York is set to join the rest of the country in legalizing mixed martial arts (MMA) fights, as the state Assembly gets ready to pass a bill lifting a ban on the full-contact sport, a measure the Senate has passed several times over the years. The lower house of the New York State Assembly is expected to vote on the legislation on Tuesday afternoon; it had long been blocked because Assembly leaders refused to let it reach the floor despite wide support among lawmakers. Its passage will allow Governor Andrew Cuomo to sign the bill into law. Cuomo, a Democrat who needs the revenue the sport would generate for his proposed budget, has already said he would sign it. New York is the only state that bans MMA, a controversial sport involving kicking, punching, wrestling and other moves that can leave fighters bloodied and sometimes unconscious. The decision to bring the bill to a vote in the Assembly comes a year after Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver stepped down in a corruption scandal. He was succeeded by a former co-sponsor of the bill, Assemblyman Carl E. Heastie, a Bronx Democrat. Michael Whyland, a spokesman for Heastie, said in an email that the floor vote is expected on Tuesday. MMA fights are expected to bring in $135 million a year for the state’s coffers, according to a 2013 study by the sport’s promoters, Ultimate Fighting Championship. Arenas across New York would benefit, and Madison Square Garden in New York City is especially well suited to host the bouts, the bill’s sponsors say. Cuomo has already included $3 million in revenue from ticket sales and cable fees in his proposed budget for the next fiscal year.

The NFL has denied the Dallas Cowboys' request to wear the Arm-in-Arm decal on their helmets for Saturday's preseason opener against the Los Angeles Rams. The Cowboys had unveiled the decal at an emotional start to their first padded practice of training camp, when they walked arm-in-arm on the field with Dallas police officials, including police chief David Brown, Dallas Mayor Mike Rawlings and the families of the police officers slain in the line of duty last month. The Cowboys, who wear the decal on their helmets during training camp, knew they would not be able to wear the decal for the regular season but had hoped to wear it in the preseason. “We certainly understand the position the league takes on this, but it won't diminish our support for that concept of unity and supporting our police force and what they do to make our lives better on a daily basis,” coach Jason Garrett said. “That arm-in-arm image is something that we really believe in. You heard me talk about it a couple weeks back. What we're trying to do as a football team is build a team that's close. We talk a lot about unity and having each other's backs, and certainly they embody that.” Cowboys owner Jerry Jones also commented on the decal controversy. Tight end Jason Witten spearheaded the idea of the players honoring the police and the families.

title: The Illusion of a Better Iran Deal
text: Some people are demanding a “better deal” than the framework nuclear agreement reached with Iran on April 2. But a better deal is a chimera, an illusory option, and it should not trick us into believing that another agreement is out there if only we pressed harder. The current agreement, which depends on key pieces being settled by the end of June, can significantly limit Iran's ability to build a nuclear weapon over the next ten years or longer, and it also sets up a dynamic that could transform the volatile Middle East. Senator Mark Kirk has delayed a vote on the Iran sanctions bill he drafted with Senator Robert Menendez, possibly until June 30. That is a constructive move that avoids a step that would undermine negotiations toward a final agreement. But we have to keep the sanctions question in view, because it is inseparable from the same calls for a better deal coming from people in Congress, Israel and other critics. Nobody can argue that a better agreement wouldn’t be better—3,000 Iranian centrifuges is better than 5,000; a 20-year deal is better than 10. The hard question is: How do you get there? Leaving aside how the Iranians might respond to more pressure—digging in deeper, speeding up their program—and looking only at our side of the equation, the idea of a better deal is unattainable. Here is why. According to critics, the pursuit of a better deal begins with ratcheting up sanctions on Iran. If tough sanctions brought them to the table, the argument goes, tougher sanctions will bring them to their knees.

title: Zika in South Florida: What We Know and What We Don’t
text: Zika transmission has been confirmed in two Miami-area neighborhoods, and pregnant women have been told to stay away from both. Federal health officials have also suggested that pregnant women and their sexual partners consider staying away from the whole Miami area. Zika infections are also occurring in Puerto Rico and in Latin American and Caribbean countries. • Most Americans have little to fear from the Zika virus. For nearly everyone, including older adults, young children and people with weakened immune systems, it is a mild illness that usually causes nothing worse than a low fever and an itchy rash. But because it can cross the placenta and attack fetal brain cells, it is dangerous to unborn children. Health officials have strongly urged pregnant women to do everything possible to avoid it. • Although thousands of Americans have come back from Latin America and the Caribbean with the virus, nearly all have recovered within a week or two. A few have passed it on to sexual partners, but in almost every case those partners have also recovered quickly. • People who have had Zika are immune to the virus. They cannot catch it again or pass it to their child. It is not yet known whether the immunity lasts for life, but it appears to. • People can also pass the virus to Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which can then spread it to other people. So far, that kind of transmission has been found in only one small area of the continental United States, in one county. How far it will spread is unknown, but diseases in that region usually start to decline only when cold weather kills the mosquitoes or makes them dormant.
